title: A case report on serendipitous diagnosis of wilson’s disease in a child with brucellosis and pseudomonal infection
case_prompt:
A 9-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of fever and jaundice. Ten days earlier she had developed intermittent fevers up to 38.9 °C with chills, yellow discoloration of the skin, dark urine, and right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. Two days before transfer, at a local hospital she was found to have a hemoglobin concentration of 3.4 g/dL, was transfused with two units of packed red blood cells, and transferred for further evaluation.

On arrival she appeared ill and tired. Temperature was 38.3 °C, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, heart rate 92 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She had conjunctival icterus and pallor. The liver was palpable 6 cm below the costal margin; the spleen tip was 1 cm below the left costal margin. There was mild right upper-quadrant tenderness; no ascites or stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Laboratory testing two days after transfusion showed hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, total bilirubin 16.3 mg/dL, prothrombin time 18.3 seconds, activated partial thromboplastin time 65 seconds, and normal serum aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels. A direct Coombs test was positive. Tests for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatomegaly with coarse echotexture, mild splenomegaly, and minimal ascites. Intravenous fluids and empiric antibiotics were started.

On hospital day 3, Brucella serology was 1:160 and blood cultures grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa. At that time, aspartate aminotransferase was 76 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 52 U/L, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, prothrombin time 20 seconds, and activated partial thromboplastin time 63 seconds. Antibiotics were changed to cefepime, doxycycline, and rifampin.

On hospital day 5, she received two more units of packed red blood cells for a hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL. Although total bilirubin decreased briefly after starting the new antibiotics, liver function tests then worsened, with rising total and indirect bilirubin levels, transaminases, and prothrombin time/international normalized ratio.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Brucellosis considered — “Exposure to milked animals including a bovine calf raised the suspicion of Brucellosis whereas source of Pseudomonas bacteremia was not entirely clear.”  
2. Pseudomonas bacteremia considered — “blood culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa.”  
3. Viral hepatitis excluded — “tests for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses were negative.”  
4. Autoimmune liver disease excluded — “Results of ANA (Anti‐Nuclear Antibody) and anti‐dsDNA (double‐stranded deoxyribonucleic acid) were unremarkable.”  
5. Drug‐induced liver injury considered — “infection might have triggered DCT negative hemolytic anemia resulting in progressive jaundice, and antibiotics treatment might have initially lowered the severity of hemolysis… but later worsening of liver function test could have been from use of hepatotoxic drugs like doxycycline … and rifampin.”  
6. Wilson’s disease considered — “liver function continued to get worse despite appropriate antibiotic treatment which raised the possibility of other causes of liver failure including autoimmune liver disease and Wilson's disease.”  
7. Wilson’s disease confirmed — “Based on a low serum ceruloplasmin and high urinary copper excretion, diagnosis of Wilson's disease was established.”
